title: Nothing Personal

jokes.text: That sign says 'apple sauce.' No, no, no. I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'
jokes.setup: Warm-up guy points to the applause sign and deadpans that it says 'apple sauce'
jokes.punchline: Immediate self-correction — 'No, no, no. I'm kidding. It says applause.' — a classic audience warm-up gag that acknowledges the artificiality of the applause cue
jokes.explanation: A functional warm-up room joke that has been used in some form since variety TV began. Mild meta-awareness of the studio audience apparatus, but entirely generic. Not a Larry Sanders joke so much as a background texture joke establishing the world.

dialogue.speaker: Warm-up comedian
dialogue.line: That sign says, 'apple sauce.' No, no, no. I'm kidding. It says, 'applause.'

jokes.text: And now, because there's nowhere left to run, Larry Sanders!
jokes.setup: The standard hyperbolic late-night announcer intro builds to the host's entrance
jokes.punchline: 'Because there's nowhere left to run' — subverts the triumphant intro formula with a bleak, fatalistic spin implying Larry is trapped in his own show
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp piece of showbiz satire compressed into one line. The announcer intro is a sacred late-night convention, and dropping 'nowhere left to run' recontextualizes it as existential dread. It also perfectly characterizes Hank — he delivers it with complete professionalism, the bleakness slipped in under the radar. High economy, strong character integration. A rewatch bonus because on first viewing it might register as a quirky line; on rewatch you feel how perfectly it encapsulates the whole show's thesis.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And now, because there's nowhere left to run, Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: Trust me, your response only means you have to get out of the house more.
jokes.setup: Audience applauds loudly as Larry takes the stage; he acknowledges the warm reception
jokes.punchline: He deflects the enthusiasm by diagnosing the audience as shut-ins rather than accepting the compliment — simultaneously self-deprecating and condescending
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders neurotic deflection — he can't accept praise without undermining it. The joke works because it's simultaneously a put-down of the audience AND a self-put-down (implying his show is only exciting to people with no social life). Strong character integration because this exact move is quintessentially Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Trust me, your response only means you have to get out of the house more.

jokes.text: Shannon Faulkner has quit. She is said to be devastated, and really has no idea where she will find a husband now.
jokes.setup: Larry reports the news item about Shannon Faulkner quitting The Citadel military academy after two years of court battles
jokes.punchline: The punchline pivots from her military ambitions to a reductive sexist joke about husband-hunting — a parody of the cultural framing of women's ambition
jokes.explanation: A topical monologue joke of the era — the kind that Carson or Leno would deliver. The comedic logic is that it punctures Faulkner's feminist milestone with a retrograde punchline, but it's more mean-spirited than clever. It functions as a parody of late-night monologue hack-ery, which gives it slight meta-value in context, but it's still a weak joke on its own merits.

dialogue.line: She is said to be devastated, and really has no idea where she will find a husband now.

jokes.text: I think it was really the stress of dragging, you know, that big, fat ass through the obstacle course.
jokes.setup: Larry builds a more sympathetic reading of Faulkner's quit — 'she said it was the stress of being alone and the 2 years of court battles'
jokes.punchline: He abandons the sympathetic framing and goes straight for a body-shaming punchline, escalating into cruder territory after the first Shannon Faulkner joke
jokes.explanation: This is deliberately hack late-night monologue material — the 'fat ass' punchline is exactly what a mediocre TV host would land on. In context, this works as a satirical portrait of lazy monologue writing, but as a standalone joke it's cheap and unoriginal. The false-feint setup ('I was actually fascinated') before the brutal deflation has some structure value, but the punchline itself is just a body-shaming cheap shot.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think it was really the stress of dragging, you know, that big, fat ass through the obstacle course.

jokes.text: He told her not to tell anyone, but evidently it slipped out at a pep rally.
jokes.setup: Congressman Mel Reynolds convicted of having sex with a 16-year-old; he told her not to tell anyone
jokes.punchline: 'Slipped out at a pep rally' — wordplay implying both that the secret got out AND a crude double-entendre about the sex act itself
jokes.explanation: A competent topical monologue joke with a serviceable double-entendre. The construction is clean — the double meaning of 'slipped out' does real work — but it's still fundamentally a low-craft late-night political sex scandal joke. The 'pep rally' specificity gives it a little extra snap.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Boy, he told her not to tell anyone, but evidently it slipped out at a pep rally.

jokes.text: They will be converted to taxis by spitting on the windshields, slashing the seats, and putting used condoms down on the floor.
jokes.setup: NYC approved 100 brand-new minivans to be converted to taxicabs; they're standard factory minivans
jokes.punchline: The 'conversion' is achieved by applying the disgusting characteristics of existing NYC cabs — escalating from gross (spit) to worse (slashed seats) to darkly filthy (used condoms)
jokes.explanation: This is the best monologue joke of the three. The list structure is perfectly executed: it escalates properly (the third item, used condoms, lands hardest), and the comedic conceit — that the 'conversion' is just degradation — is a clean, efficient inversion. The observational premise about NYC cab filth is dated but the construction is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They're actually standard, normal, factory minivans that will be converted to taxis by spitting on the windshields, slashing the seats, and putting used condoms down on the floor.

jokes.text: Melissa Gilbert. Oh, for Christ's sake. How are you gonna generate some heat around Melissa Gilbert? / Ladies and gentlemen, Melissa Gilbert! Wa-hoo!
jokes.setup: Artie asks Paula for a big guest suggestion to get the network off his back; Paula offers Melissa Gilbert
jokes.punchline: Artie's volcanic dismissal followed by a staff member doing a limp mock-announcement with zero enthusiasm ('Wa-hoo!') perfectly captures the room's collective disdain
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed piece of industry comedy: the gap between the inflated mock-announcement form and the absolute deflation of 'Wa-hoo!' is perfectly timed. Artie's 'for Christ's sake' is character-perfect. The joke functions on Hollywood industry insider knowledge — Melissa Gilbert in 1995 is a punchline that requires no explanation to the right audience.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Melissa gilbert.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, for Christ's sake. How are you gonna generate some heat around Melissa gilbert? Ladies and gentlemen, Melissa gilbert! Wa-hoo!

jokes.text: Who in hell is Michael Chiklis? The Commish. No, that was my imitation of America.
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Michael Chiklis; Artie asks who he is; someone answers 'The Commish'
jokes.punchline: 'No, that was my imitation of America' — Artie reframes his baffled question as a parody of a culturally oblivious nation, turning ignorance into a meta-commentary on mainstream TV taste
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest lines in the episode. The structure is pristine: Artie asks a genuine question, gets an answer, then retroactively claims his question was satire rather than ignorance — rescuing his dignity while also scoring a legitimate point about network TV mediocrity. 'My imitation of America' is a devastatingly economical insult that works on multiple levels: it's a dig at The Commish's popularity, at mainstream audiences, and at network executives. Highly quotable, completely character-specific to Artie's patrician contempt. Comparable to an 8.0 reference point.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Michael chiklis.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Who in hell is Michael chiklis?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: The commish.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No, that was my imitation of America. Who the hell is Michael chiklis?

jokes.text: Jeff Goldblum is great. He's always been on our most wanted list. Except for every time I ask his agent, he passes.
jokes.setup: Paula suggests Jeff Goldblum; everyone enthusiastically agrees he'd be great
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate pivot — 'except for every time I ask his agent, he passes' — undermines the enthusiasm cold
jokes.explanation: A clean deflation joke. The rhythm of build-up ('always been on our most wanted list') followed by immediate crash ('passes every time') is efficiently structured. The subtext — that even the show's most-wanted guests can't be bothered — is delicious industry satire.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: So we don't have him?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We don't have him, but I thought since you were friends with him, you could ask him.

jokes.text: Why don't you ask one of your friends? OK. I'll ask my friend Jill. Great. Jill who? You don't know her. She works at Killer Shrimp.
jokes.setup: Artie suggests Larry ask his friend Jeff Goldblum; Larry deflects by suggesting Artie ask one of his own friends
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'friend' turns out to be a woman who works at a restaurant called Killer Shrimp — the bathos of a show business power broker's social circle bottoming out at a shrimp joint employee is the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke works on character — Artie is usually the all-knowing veteran, so revealing he has no famous friends of his own is a puncture. 'Killer Shrimp' as the specific restaurant name does extra work (it's a real L.A. chain, adding a layer of specificity that makes it funnier than a generic diner). The beat builds quickly and pays off well.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why don't you ask one of your friends?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: OK. I'll ask my friend Jill.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Great. Jill who?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: You don't know her. She works at killer shrimp.

jokes.text: I have that on a poster with a little kitty hanging off a bar. Yeah? Have you seen the poster that says, 'A rule is a rule, and I'm sitting on a toilet'?
jokes.setup: Artie delivers a motivational speech about taking risks ('That's what life's all about?'); Larry sarcastically says it sounds like an inspirational poster
jokes.punchline: Larry one-ups with an imaginary poster of his own — 'a rule is a rule, and I'm sitting on a toilet' — a perfectly absurd non-sequitur that doubles as self-defense
jokes.explanation: This exchange is one of the episode's comedic high points. The setup (Artie's motivational speech, Artie's poster response) is good, but Larry's counter — the toilet poster — is inspired. The absurdism is precise: it's not random, it's Larry asserting his stubbornness through the most undignified image possible. 'I'm sitting on a toilet' is Larry Sanders in a sentence — neurotic, self-aware, refusing to be moved while in an embarrassing position. Strong character integration; the line could only come from Larry defending a petty personal rule.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I have that on a poster with a little kitty hanging off a bar.

jokes.text: Or, as I call him, the Knish.
jokes.setup: Susan (the publicist) looks at the guest list and someone says 'Michael Chiklis' — 'the Commish'
jokes.punchline: Artie offers his personal nickname: 'the Knish' — a Jewish deli food pun on 'the Commish' that perfectly skewers the show's pretensions through one absurd food rhyme
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical callback. 'The Knish' does three things at once: it's a wordplay rhyme, it's Artie's Jewish New York sensibility sneaking in, and it's an implicit dismissal (a knish is a humble snack food — not exactly a star). One word, maximum return. Perfectly characteristic of Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Have you seen the poster that says, 'a rule is a rule, and I'm sitting on a toilet'?

jokes.text: Michael Chiklis has done a movie — he was in 'Wired' a few years ago. John Belushi. He played John Belushi. Oh, big loss. What a tragedy. Yes, but I wish he was alive and here and on the show tonight.
jokes.setup: Michael Chiklis is defended on the basis of his movie role; he played John Belushi in 'Wired' (the controversial biopic)
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'big loss, what a tragedy' sounds like he means Belushi's death — but Susan's pivot ('I wish he was alive and here and on the show tonight') clarifies the real tragedy is that Belushi CAN'T be booked, reframing death as a booking inconvenience
jokes.explanation: A sharp piece of showbiz dark comedy: the room's only regret about Belushi's death is the booking problem it creates. The pivot from 'big loss, what a tragedy' (which lands as genuine sentiment) to 'I wish he was alive and here on the show' (which reframes tragedy as a scheduling inconvenience) is characteristic of the show's industry-insider nihilism.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Melissa gilbert.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yahoo.

jokes.text: I'd settle for Freddie Prinze at this point.
jokes.setup: The booking crisis deepens; Larry has already half-joked about wishing Belushi were alive to do the show
jokes.punchline: Larry escalates the dead-celebrity booking fantasy by adding another deceased star — Freddie Prinze — doubling down on the show's willingness to treat death as a talent availability issue
jokes.explanation: The escalation from Belushi to Freddie Prinze (another celebrity who died young by suicide, which gives it a slightly darker edge) is well-timed. The joke's economy is excellent — four words after sufficient context do a lot of dark work. The callback structure amplifies the original joke's conceit cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Or, as I call him, the knish.

jokes.text: She had a 2-year relationship with a grip at ABC and an intense week with Scott Bakula, and just ended a very painful relationship with Macgyver.
jokes.setup: Hank asks if Susan (the publicist) is single; Artie rattles off her relationship history
jokes.punchline: The escalating absurdity of the relationship résumé — from a grip (below-the-line crew) to a TV star, with Artie treating celebrity and civilian relationships with equal tabloid authority, capped by 'Macgyver' (the character name rather than Richard Dean Anderson)
jokes.explanation: The joke works on Artie's omniscience (he knows everyone's business) and on the showbiz ecosystem specificity — a grip at ABC, Scott Bakula, then 'MacGyver.' Using the character name instead of the actor's name is a nice touch of industry-insider absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yes, but I wish he was alive and here and on the show tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Yeah. So do I. I'd settle for freddie prinze at this point.

jokes.text: So the MacGyver thing's over? Kaput.
jokes.setup: Beverly has listed Susan's ex as 'MacGyver'
jokes.punchline: Hank asks if the 'MacGyver thing is over' — treating MacGyver as the actual name, playing it completely straight
jokes.explanation: Hank's earnestness in treating 'MacGyver' as a legitimate name for the ex continues the bit naturally. The one-word 'Kaput' from Beverly is a nice economy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: She had a 2-year relationship with a grip at abc and an intense week with Scott bakula, and just ended a very painful relationship with macgyver.

jokes.text: You know, goddamn him and that talking car. No, no, no. That's David Hasselhoff. Macgyver's the... Richard Dean Anderson. Well, what does Macgyver do? He makes stuff out of nothing. Oh. What does that mean? Is he a drama queen?
jokes.setup: Hank blames 'Macgyver' for Susan's heartbreak; Artie corrects him — the talking car is Hasselhoff (Knight Rider), not MacGyver
jokes.punchline: Hank's confusion between two '80s TV heroes is funny enough; his follow-up question 'he makes stuff out of nothing — is he a drama queen?' completely misunderstands MacGyver's iconic skill set as a personality disorder
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully layered exchange. The first beat (Hank confusing MacGyver and Knight Rider) is strong character comedy — Hank's showbiz knowledge has a very specific ceiling. The second beat ('he makes stuff out of nothing — is he a drama queen?') is the real payoff: a literal misreading of MacGyver's defining trait reframed as emotional manipulation. It's a non-sequitur that follows its own perfect internal logic. Highly character-specific to Hank's particular brand of oblivious grandeur.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: what the fuck are you talking about? I don't want to ask her.

jokes.text: Well, you should find out if she'll go out with me. May I please leave? No. Will you find out if she'll go out with me?
jokes.setup: Larry wants Artie to ask Susan out on his behalf
jokes.punchline: Artie asks to leave; Larry says no and repeats the request — treating his producer like a middle-school messenger
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the power dynamic: Larry is the boss but he's behaving like a 14-year-old asking his friend to pass a note. Artie's 'May I please leave?' is a beautifully formal way to register contempt. Character-dependent and earned.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: If I didn't work for him, I'd be all over that.

jokes.text: Brian? I haven't seen Brian all day. Have you? No, I haven't seen him. You would've thought Brian would've mentioned Hank was coming in. Yeah, you would've thought so.
jokes.setup: Hank enters Larry's office unexpectedly, wanting emotional support for his divorce; Larry and his assistant perform mutual surprise that their assistant Brian failed to warn them
jokes.punchline: The extended, knowing exchange about Brian's failure is a thin cover — it's obvious they're trying to avoid dealing with Hank, and the audience sees the transparent avoidance while Hank stands there
jokes.explanation: A classic Larry Sanders cringe beat. Larry and Beverly conspire openly in front of Hank, performing ignorance about Brian while Hank stands waiting for emotional support. The joke is the sustained awkwardness and the transparency of the dodge. Strong character integration — this is exactly how Larry avoids emotional confrontation.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know, goddamn him and that talking car. No, no, no. That's David Hasselhoff. Macgyver's the... Richard Dean Anderson.

jokes.text: Larry interrupts Hank's emotional divorce confession to take a phone call about a tape hold ('Larry Sanders, 551. All clear.')
jokes.setup: Hank has finally cornered Larry for emotional support about his divorce ('this'll just take a second'); Larry is visibly looking for an out
jokes.punchline: The phone rings and Larry immediately answers — a tape logistics call — while Hank waits mid-sentence; Larry dismisses the call and returns to Hank as if nothing happened
jokes.explanation: A well-executed cringe beat. Larry's willingness to take a meaningless logistics call in the middle of Hank's emotional breakdown is character-perfect cowardice. The mundanity of '551, all clear' against Hank's vulnerability is the joke. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh. What does that mean? Is he a Drama queen?

jokes.text: Fucking bitch! She's going after the Lookaround Cafe. That is my baby.
jokes.setup: Hank has been building up to emotional vulnerability about his divorce; he's speaking softly about 'the bond that 2 caring people can have'
jokes.punchline: The sudden eruption — 'Fucking bitch! She's going after the Lookaround Cafe' — after the sentimental setup is a tonal whiplash that reveals Hank's 'emotional healing' is entirely self-serving
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. The pivot from 'the bond that 2 caring people can have' to 'Fucking bitch!' is perfectly timed tonal whiplash. What makes it exceptional is the specificity: she's going after the Lookaround Cafe — his restaurant, 'his baby.' Hank's emotional wound isn't about love or loss; it's about property. This is deeply character-specific: Hank's sentimentality is always really about Hank's ego. The 'fucking bitch/my baby' juxtaposition in two consecutive sentences is a miniature character study.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I can't imagine why Brian wouldn't come in here and tell us that Hank's coming in. It doesn't sound like him, does it?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I know. Wow.

jokes.text: What about the beach house? Oh, fuck the beach house. It's a rental. Well, you told everyone you owned the beach house. I do in the summer.
jokes.setup: Larry suggests Hank could at least keep the beach house in the settlement
jokes.punchline: 'I do in the summer' — Hank's breezy reclassification of renting as owning, delivered without shame, is a perfect capsule of his self-mythologizing
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. In five words ('I do in the summer'), the joke reveals Hank's entire relationship with reality: he tells people he owns the beach house because he rents it for the summer, and in his mind that's equivalent. The beat — Larry's pause absorbing this logic — is the payoff. This is among the best character jokes of the episode. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, and executed in the fewest possible words.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Larry Sanders, 551. All clear. Huh? No. Just hold that one. Thank you.

jokes.text: Take the high road. Give her whatever she wants. Thanks for being there for me.
jokes.setup: Larry, as a man twice divorced, gives Hank advice: 'Take the high road. Give her whatever she wants.'
jokes.punchline: Hank receives this devastatingly self-serving advice as though it were genuine emotional wisdom ('Thanks for being there for me'), unaware or uncaring that Larry is just trying to get rid of him quickly
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the structural gap: Larry's 'advice' is self-serving (he wants Hank to leave), Hank mistakes it for sincere counsel, and the audience watches the mutual self-deception. Solid character comedy but not the episode's sharpest.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Fucking bitch! She's going after the lookaround cafe.

jokes.text: This is no big deal. Last week they did a tribute to Steven Seagal. This is not a big deal.
jokes.setup: Everyone is congratulating Jeff Goldblum at the AFI tribute dinner, calling it a great honor
jokes.punchline: Goldblum deflates the honor by pointing out the AFI just did a tribute to Steven Seagal — implying the AFI's taste in honorees has cratered to the point where his own tribute is meaningless
jokes.explanation: A self-deprecating industry joke delivered with perfect Goldblum energy. The Steven Seagal name-drop as the nadir of AFI taste is well-chosen (Seagal in 1995 is already a cultural punchline), and the double insistence ('this is no big deal… This is not a big deal') has a nice compulsive quality suggesting Goldblum genuinely needs to say it twice.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, fuck the beach house. It's a rental.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, you told everyone you owned the beach house.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I do in the summer.

jokes.text: Buckaroo Banzai! Yes. Perfect Tommy, Rawhide, Reno, Penny Priddy. What are they all doing now? I wonder.
jokes.setup: Paula gushes over Goldblum's filmography at the AFI dinner — Ernie Kovacs, Jurassic Park, The Fly
jokes.punchline: She adds 'Buckaroo Banzai' and they both go deep into the cast roster; Goldblum's wistful 'what are they all doing now? I wonder' treats a cultishly obscure '80s film as if its ensemble were a dispersed family of peers
jokes.explanation: A gentle inside-baseball showbiz joke about Buckaroo Banzai's cult status. Goldblum's nostalgic 'I wonder what they're doing now' is a nicely understated line — it has the rhythm of genuine sentiment but signals the film's obscurity. Works best for viewers who know the reference.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This is no big deal. Last week, they did a tribute to steven seagal.

jokes.text: Oh, Paula, this is not the time or place to be asking Mr. Goldblum about a silly talk show.
jokes.setup: Paula, the talent booker, asks Goldblum directly at the AFI dinner if he'll do the show
jokes.punchline: Larry intervenes by calling his own show 'a silly talk show' — publicly humiliating Paula while simultaneously humiliating himself and the show he hosts, all to avoid the risk of Goldblum saying no to his face
jokes.explanation: A perfect cringe comedy beat. Larry's attempt to seem cool by distancing himself from his own show in front of Goldblum is transparently self-protective. Calling it 'a silly talk show' is the tell — his paranoia about rejection is so acute he'll pre-emptively humiliate himself. Strong character integration: this is Larry's defining flaw in action.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Goldblum
dialogue.line: What are they all doing now? I wonder.

jokes.text: Larry, my boy. Good morning. / Did you ask Jeff Goldblum to do the show last night? Yes. Yes, I did, but he wouldn't give me an answer. The whole evening was pretty much a big waste of time. Except for those stuffed mushrooms.
jokes.setup: Artie asks Larry about the AFI dinner and whether he invited Goldblum; Larry admits the whole evening was a waste
jokes.punchline: 'Except for those stuffed mushrooms' — the only thing Larry salvaged from the evening was the catering; the mushrooms become a payoff to an earlier scene detail and reduce the Hollywood prestige event to a food stop
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed callback. The stuffed mushrooms were mentioned in passing during the AFI scene; their return here as the only positive outcome of a networking evening is perfectly timed deflation. 'Except for those stuffed mushrooms' as the final word on a Hollywood prestige event is economical and funny. The callback gives it rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Waiter
dialogue.line: These are from the yucatán peninsula.

jokes.text: You couldn't ask him yourself, could you? No, I couldn't. And you haven't been able to ask Susan out.
jokes.setup: It emerges that Larry had Paula ask Goldblum to do the show at the AFI dinner (after refusing to ask himself)
jokes.punchline: Artie draws the parallel — Larry can't ask Goldblum directly AND can't ask Susan out directly, suggesting a comprehensive inability to do anything uncomfortable in person
jokes.explanation: A structural joke that reveals character via parallel construction. The comedy is in Artie connecting the two avoidance behaviors, making the pattern explicit. Functional but not flashy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What is wrong with you?

jokes.text: Sorry to hear about your divorce. I guess you guys in publicity are having a real good laugh. Married on TV, and a year later, cancelled.
jokes.setup: Susan offers condolences about Hank's divorce
jokes.punchline: Hank preemptively assumes the publicists are mocking him and frames his marriage's failure in TV-industry terms: 'Married on TV, and a year later, cancelled' — applying a cancellation metaphor to his marriage
jokes.explanation: A brilliant piece of character writing. Hank describing his marriage as 'cancelled' after being 'on TV' is superficially funny, but underneath it's devastating: he can only understand personal relationships through the lens of television. His entire self-concept is mediated by show business. The paranoia ('having a real good laugh') followed by the self-pity of 'cancelled' is classic Hank — defensive, grandiose, and accidentally poignant. Highly quotable, strong originality.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I guess you guys in publicity are having a real good laugh. Married on TV, and a year later, cancelled.

jokes.text: I'm giving her the restaurant in the settlement. Really? Well, that's very generous of you. Well, I've decided to take the high road. Any chance we could use that to make her look like a cunt?
jokes.setup: Hank tells Susan he's taking the 'high road' and giving his wife the restaurant — referencing Larry's advice from earlier
jokes.punchline: 'Any chance we could use that to make her look like a cunt?' — Hank has taken the high road purely as a PR strategy and immediately asks the publicist to weaponize his generosity
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: Larry gave Hank the 'high road' advice as a means of dismissal; Hank genuinely internalized it but immediately revealed his actual goal — to use apparent generosity as a PR weapon against his ex-wife. The callback to Larry's advice, the PR context (asking the publicist), the vulgar specificity of 'make her look like a cunt,' and the delivery (Hank is entirely sincere and business-like about it) combine for maximum impact. This is character comedy at its finest: a single sentence reveals Hank's ego, his vindictiveness, his media-savviness, and his total lack of self-awareness simultaneously. Comparable to or exceeding the Snip-Snap anchor in character specificity and structural elegance.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Any chance we could use that to make her look like a cunt?

jokes.text: Uh, maybe. Let me sleep on that one, Hank.
jokes.setup: Hank has just asked Susan if she can use his restaurant gift to make his wife look bad
jokes.punchline: Susan's non-committal 'Uh, maybe. Let me sleep on that one' treats the monstrous request as a normal professional task requiring only a brief think — no shock, no refusal, just a publicist's pragmatic pause
jokes.explanation: The perfect coda to joke #30. Susan's response is entirely in deadpan — she doesn't recoil, she doesn't refuse, she treats it like a tricky PR brief. This characterizes the entire entertainment publicist world as morally flexible professionals who will 'sleep on' using generosity to weaponize someone's reputation. The restraint of the response is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: From what?

jokes.text: Do you have any interest in going out with Larry? (Susan asked by Hank's assistant/secretary)
jokes.setup: The running gag of Larry's proxies asking Susan out on his behalf continues — first Beverly, then Hank, now another staff member
jokes.punchline: The escalating absurdity of yet another person being deployed to ask Susan out; the question is delivered flatly as if it's a normal work errand
jokes.explanation: The third iteration of the running gag has diminishing joke-per-iteration returns but the sheer accumulation is funny. The joke is now fully structural — we're laughing at the pattern rather than the individual ask.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A huge fucking baby. We're talkin' about, uh, Hank, right?

jokes.text: My good buddy Ricardo Montalban won't be joining us this evening. He's on vacation. From what?
jokes.setup: Artie reports that Ricardo Montalban has declined; he's on vacation
jokes.punchline: 'From what?' — Larry's genuine puzzlement about what a retired character actor could possibly be on vacation from is a perfect delivery of the absurdist premise. Montalban exists in a state of perpetual vacation; the concept of him needing a break from nothing is the joke
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum return. 'From what?' is a masterclass in comedic economy — it requires no setup explanation (the Montalban running gag has been established) and the single-question punchline does everything: it characterizes Larry's obliviousness, it punctures the idea that aging TV stars have active careers, and it lands as a genuine absurdist moment. One of the episode's most quotable micro-moments.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And listen. Seriously, you must feel free to say no if this is not something you want to do. You're a love. That's what I love about you. You're my hero, see?

jokes.text: I just bumped into Hank in the crapper — Artie, I'm trying to eat oatmeal here. Please.
jokes.setup: Artie relays Hank's message; he mentions he bumped into him 'in the crapper'
jokes.punchline: Larry is eating oatmeal; 'the crapper' as a location detail is sufficient to ruin the meal — Larry's squeamishness (while eating, no less) is character-consistent
jokes.explanation: A small physical-comedy-adjacent cringe beat. The timing is good but it's a minor joke — functional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Goldblum
dialogue.line: I've been waiting for you to ask me. I mean, you know, I was hoping to do the show, and last night, you know, with the booker, when she asked me, you got all funny with her.

jokes.text: He wants you to know that Susan is too busy. For what? To go out with you. How would he know that? Because you asked him to ask her.
jokes.setup: Artie relays Hank's message: Susan is too busy
jokes.punchline: The relay chain — Larry asked Hank, Hank asked Susan, Hank told Artie, Artie is telling Larry — has become a 4-person telephone game for a simple date request, and Artie's flat recounting of this bureaucratic romantic failure is devastating
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the absurd bureaucratic infrastructure Larry has built to avoid a single direct conversation. Artie's deadpan navigation of the relay chain — 'Because you asked him to ask her' — functions as dry commentary on Larry's emotional cowardice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Goldblum
dialogue.line: No, and take your shit show and shove it up your big, fat ass?

jokes.text: Well, I guess some people are not as good as you are in confronting people face to face. No. He has to have somebody do his little dirty work for him, doesn't he? What a baby. A huge fucking baby. We're talkin' about Hank, right? Who do you think we're talking about?
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are discussing Hank going through Artie to deliver Susan's rejection message, rather than telling Larry directly
jokes.punchline: Larry goes on an escalating rant about 'huge fucking baby' behavior and the need for proxies — while being entirely unaware he is describing himself (he also uses proxies for everything). Artie's question 'We're talkin' about Hank, right?' lands as a precision needle-prick
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent piece of ironic character comedy. The entire joke is that Larry is righteously condemning Hank for doing the exact same thing Larry does throughout the episode (using proxies). Artie's needle of 'we're talkin' about Hank, right?' is perfectly placed — it invites the audience to make the connection without spelling it out. The irony is total, and it's earned because the episode has carefully built the parallel. One of the episode's standout structural moments.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Pussy alert! Pussy alert! Susan's here. She's coming on the hot asphalt.

jokes.text: And listen. Seriously, you must feel free to say no if this is not something you want to do. You're a love. That's what I love about you. You're my hero, see?
jokes.setup: Larry has finally called Goldblum directly; he's asking him to do the show 'tonight' but front-loading with so many disclaimers and compliments that the actual ask keeps getting buried
jokes.punchline: Goldblum's enthusiastic 'You're my hero' before he even knows what he's being asked is warm-up flattery that makes the subsequent ask (do the show TONIGHT?) even more cringingly presumptuous
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe beat. The gap between the elaborate compliment-hedging and the audacity of the actual request (tonight!) creates the tension. Larry's social cowardice is on full display, but the scene is building toward a bigger payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Pussy alerts are just not as much fun as they used to be.

jokes.text: Like tonight. Larry. Tonight, really? Well, I... / I've been waiting for you to ask me.
jokes.setup: After elaborate hedging, Larry finally asks Goldblum to do the show — 'like tonight'
jokes.punchline: Goldblum's 'I've been waiting for you to ask me' completely deflates the tension — he was always going to say yes, and all of Larry's anxiety and proxies and diplomatic maneuvering were entirely unnecessary
jokes.explanation: A well-earned structural payoff. The entire Goldblum subplot — the rule about not asking friends, Paula's embarrassing ask at the AFI dinner, Larry's call — has been building to this: Goldblum was happy to do the show all along. The joke retroactively devalues all of Larry's anxiety as self-created. The misdirection is elegant because Goldblum's cheerfulness makes the waste of effort funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Doing everybody's job.

jokes.text: No, and take your shit show and shove it up your big, fat ass?
jokes.setup: Goldblum is explaining that he was always going to say yes; Larry was confused that he got 'funny' when Paula asked at the AFI dinner
jokes.punchline: Goldblum voice-acts the rejection Larry apparently feared — 'No, and take your shit show and shove it up your big, fat ass?' — a hyperbolic version of Larry's paranoid worst-case scenario, delivered cheerfully by Goldblum
jokes.explanation: A great meta-joke. Goldblum performs Larry's paranoid fantasy rejection to show how absurd it was, and the vulgarity of the imagined rejection is disproportionate to any real-world risk. 'Your shit show' and 'big fat ass' also echo the monologue's crude register, giving the episode a nice thematic through-line about the gap between Larry's self-image and his fears.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: and Phil. Phil. Huh? Phil got you already?

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Yeah, he did.

jokes.text: Great! So, we'll see you, uh, later today? Yes, I can't wait. Splendid, my boy. God. You see? When you do it yourself, you get results.
jokes.setup: Larry successfully books Goldblum and hangs up; Artie is present
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'when you do it yourself, you get results' is a perfectly placed ironic needle — Larry barely did it himself (he had Paula ask at the dinner, failed, then finally called), and Artie is giving him credit for exactly the thing he almost didn't do
jokes.explanation: A functional irony beat. Artie's lesson-learned cheerleading is ironic because Larry's 'doing it himself' came only after extensive failure with proxies. Clean but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm up at 9:30, right at the crack of, uh...

jokes.text: Pussy alert! Pussy alert! Susan's here. She's coming on the hot asphalt.
jokes.setup: Someone spots Susan arriving at the studio
jokes.punchline: The mock military/nature-documentary framing of a woman walking across the parking lot — 'pussy alert' repeated, 'on the hot asphalt' — is presented with complete institutional seriousness, making it both ridiculous and revealing about the workplace culture
jokes.explanation: The joke functions as workplace satire — a professional environment where a female colleague's arrival triggers an animal-documentary alert. The comedy is in the institutional deadpan, but 'pussy alert' itself is a blunt instrument. Gets a laugh more from audacity than craft.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't want to.

jokes.text: Larry, you want me to get your binoculars? Yeah. And my camouflage pants.
jokes.setup: Staff are watching Susan cross the parking lot; someone offers to get Larry's binoculars
jokes.punchline: 'And my camouflage pants' — Larry escalates the hunting/surveillance metaphor to full military absurdism, requesting camouflage to observe a woman walking 50 feet
jokes.explanation: The camouflage pants is a good absurdist escalation — it follows logically from the military/hunting frame but pushes it far enough to become ridiculous. The economy is excellent: one piece of requested equipment extends the gag perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey. Goldbl... is it 'blum' or 'bloom'? It's, uh, 'bloom,' oh. Well, welcome to the show.

jokes.text: Pussy alerts are just not as much fun as they used to be.
jokes.setup: Larry leaves the group to go talk to Susan himself (an unprecedented act of directness for Larry)
jokes.punchline: Phil's melancholy observation that the pussy alert has been deflated by Larry's unexpected action — the joke is the staff member's genuine disappointment that the ritual has lost its joy
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and timing. The line lands because it treats an absurd workplace ritual with genuine nostalgia. 'Just not as much fun as they used to be' implies an entire history of previous pussy alerts that the character has enjoyed, now diminished. The melancholy deadpan is perfect. One of the more quotable supporting character lines of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Goldblum
dialogue.line: Like 2 lovebirds in a cherry tree.

jokes.text: Pussy alerts are just not as much fun as they used to be.
jokes.setup: Larry has abandoned the 'pussy alert' festivities to go talk to Susan directly; Hank is left standing alone
jokes.punchline: Hank's melancholy observation that pussy alerts have lost their joy — the joke is in his genuine wistfulness about this
jokes.explanation: This is a standout line. The joke operates on multiple levels: it's Hank being abandoned (small comedy of rejection), it's a divorced man's elegy for boyish fun, and it's an absurdist observation about the diminishing returns of juvenile behavior. The sentence structure — 'just not as much fun as they used to be' — is perfect, implying a rich history of pussy alerts that have gradually soured. Strongly character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: maybe book David viscott. Viscott! 2 t's.

jokes.text: I asked him to do the show. Uh-huh. Doing everybody's job.
jokes.setup: Larry tells Susan he personally got Jeff Goldblum for tonight's show, presenting this as a notable achievement
jokes.punchline: Susan's 'doing everybody's job' is deadpan — she knows he spent the whole morning routing everything through proxies, so his finally doing one task himself is being received as heroic labor
jokes.explanation: A gentle irony beat. Susan's dry observation tags Larry's minimal effort as performative industriousness. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, you should know there was a shooting and a beating and a killing and a stabbing there.

jokes.text: And Phil. Phil. Huh? Phil got you already?
jokes.setup: Larry is confessing to Susan that Beverly and Hank both asked her out on his behalf
jokes.punchline: Susan reveals that Phil ALSO asked her out for Larry — a third proxy Larry apparently didn't even know about, making the proxy network autonomous and self-organizing
jokes.explanation: The best iteration of the running gag. The joke escalates to a new level because Larry didn't even deploy Phil — the proxy network has grown beyond his control, with staff members spontaneously asking Susan out on his behalf. 'Phil got you already?' is Larry's horrified realization that his romantic embarrassment has become a collective enterprise. The escalation is earned and the payoff is funnier than the previous iterations.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't want to.

jokes.text: Um... oh. Well, uh... heh heh. I mean, it doesn't have to be tonight if this is sort of short notice. It could be, you know, another night.
jokes.setup: Larry has finally asked Susan to dinner directly; she pauses; he immediately begins backpedaling before she's even answered
jokes.punchline: Larry's anxious pre-emptive retreat mid-invitation — offering her an out before she's spoken — is a perfect visual/verbal cringe moment revealing his terror of rejection
jokes.explanation: A strong cringe moment. The joke is in the timing — Larry hasn't even been rejected yet when he starts offering her an escape route. Character-specific and well-observed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't want to.

jokes.text: I'm so bushed. I go home, I go to sleep immediately. I understand. It's a dull existence.
jokes.setup: Susan gently declines dinner — she's exhausted after work
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'It's a dull existence' is a perfect passive-aggressive non-response to her rejection — presented as sympathetic understanding but inflected with just enough edge to sting
jokes.explanation: A beautifully loaded line. 'It's a dull existence' could be sympathetic or devastating, and the ambiguity is the joke. Larry saying it to the woman who just turned him down lands somewhere between wounded and dismissive. Strong character integration — it's precisely how Larry processes rejection.

jokes.text: I barely get enough sleep myself. I'm up at 9:30, right at the crack of, uh...
jokes.setup: Susan explains she goes home and goes to sleep immediately because she's exhausted; Larry tries to relate
jokes.punchline: 'I'm up at 9:30, right at the crack of, uh...' — Larry trails off, realizing 9:30 AM is not remotely early, exposing the enormous gap between his talk show host schedule and Susan's actual work hours
jokes.explanation: A great character-specific beat. Larry's attempted empathy crumbles mid-sentence when he realizes his 9:30 wake-up is not 'the crack of dawn.' The trailing '...uh' is perfect — he catches himself. This is quintessential Larry: tone-deaf attempts at connection that inadvertently reveal his privilege.

jokes.text: You know, it's nothing personal. It really isn't. I get up early. Didn't take it that way. Yeah, good.
jokes.setup: Susan clarifies that turning Larry down is 'nothing personal' — the episode's title phrase
jokes.punchline: Larry's insistence that he 'didn't take it that way' followed by 'yeah, good' is the opposite of convincing — the title-drop in the context of a plainly devastating rejection is darkly funny, and both characters know they're performing detachment they don't feel
jokes.explanation: The episode title delivered in context is a meta-joke for attentive viewers. The phrase 'nothing personal' is comedy in itself when used to soften a personal rejection delivered face-to-face. Larry's 'didn't take it that way' is clearly false, and the audience sees through both of them. Strong character integration — Larry's inability to admit hurt is as defining as his inability to ask directly for what he wants.

jokes.text: You need to be protected, and that's my fault, because I should've asked her to go out with you, very insensitive of me. Fucking… fucking mean. And I'm just begging you to accept my apology.
jokes.setup: Larry has returned to Artie after being rejected by Susan in person; he's wounded
jokes.punchline: Artie's elaborate apology for failing to protect Larry from the discomfort of being rejected by someone he asked out in person — the joke is that Artie is apologizing for Larry's own direct action, treating Larry's agency as something dangerous that needs to be buffered
jokes.explanation: A terrific ironic reversal. Artie just told Larry 'when you do it yourself, you get results' — and now he's apologizing for allowing Larry to do it himself. The 180 reveals Artie's real function: protecting Larry from reality. 'Fucking... fucking mean' as Artie's assessment of Susan's gentle rejection is beautifully disproportionate.

jokes.text: Don't want to. (Larry's response to being told they have a show to do)
jokes.setup: Artie transitions to work mode: 'we've got a show to do'
jokes.punchline: Larry's petulant 'Don't want to' — an adult professional refusing his own show like a sulking child — is played completely deadpan
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly placed. 'Don't want to' is the most economical expression of Larry's ego and fragility — a late-night talk show host refusing to do his own show because a woman turned him down. The delivery as a flat, childlike statement (not even a tantrum) makes it funnier. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Hey, sweetheart, you know who's out there? Jeff Goldblum, your good buddy. Come on. Come on with me, sweetheart. Let's say hello to him. Don't want to. You don't want to? No.
jokes.setup: Artie tries to coax Larry out of his funk by invoking the friend Larry just worked so hard to book
jokes.punchline: Larry refuses to see even Jeff Goldblum — the guest he spent the entire episode maneuvering to get — because he's sulking. The 'don't want to' from before becomes a running escalation
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'don't want to' and the irony of Larry refusing to see the guest he worked all episode to book deepens the character joke. Good escalation of the sulk.

jokes.text: So, how's everything going with Laura Dern? 'Cause in relationships a lot of times have a lot of ups and downs, so you guys, you know, up or down? Going up. You're up. Great.
jokes.setup: Larry and Goldblum have a pre-show green room chat; Larry asks about Goldblum's relationship with Laura Dern
jokes.punchline: Larry's phrasing ('a lot of times have a lot of ups and downs, so... up or down?') is comically meandering — he's trying to probe whether Goldblum's relationship is in trouble (possibly to feel better about his own failed date) and the question barely holds together grammatically, culminating in the blunt 'up or down?'
jokes.explanation: A nice cringe beat. Larry's transparent fishing for Goldblum's relationship to be in trouble (subconscious misery-loves-company) is delivered through barely coherent syntax. 'Up or down?' as a relationship status binary is both funny and a little sad.

jokes.text: I must tell you that, uh, Jurassic Park, it just changed my life. Which is my dressing room? Uh, 3, on the right.
jokes.setup: Hank greets Goldblum with an effusive compliment about Jurassic Park changing his life
jokes.punchline: Goldblum's response — completely ignoring the compliment and asking about his dressing room — is a perfectly cold celebrity-to-announcer dismissal; Hank's sincere flattery bounces off Goldblum's practical indifference
jokes.explanation: A clean comedy of status. Hank's obsequious compliment ('changed my life') followed by Goldblum's complete non-acknowledgment and logistical question exposes the hierarchy of the entertainment world. The joke is Goldblum's perfect indifference, which reveals that 'Jurassic Park changed my life' registers as background noise to a movie star. Strong character comedy for both characters.

jokes.text: Is it too bright in here for you? Huh? Oh, sorry.
jokes.setup: Larry, still sulking, meets Goldblum in the green room; Goldblum notices Larry seems down
jokes.punchline: Larry's response to noticing Goldblum's signature light-sensitivity tic ('Is it too bright in here for you?') as a conversational opener when Goldblum is the one who should be asking if Larry is okay — the misdirection of emotional concern is funny
jokes.explanation: A minor deflection beat. 'Is it too bright in here for you?' as an opener when Larry is the one who looks devastated is a small ironic inversion, but it doesn't land as hard as the scene's better moments.

jokes.text: Listen, we're gonna have dinner after the show. Do you want to join us? Oh, I'd love to. Yes. Thank you. Great. Great. And you, too. You come, too. We'll make it the four of us.
jokes.setup: Goldblum invites Susan to dinner; Susan accepts; Goldblum then also invites Larry — making it a foursome
jokes.punchline: Larry is now being included in a dinner that Susan declined when he asked her — and it's being offered by a third party. The dinner that was 'nothing personal' to refuse is suddenly possible when Goldblum organizes it.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully arranged ironic reversal. Susan said no to dinner with Larry; Jeff Goldblum says 'and you too, Larry' and suddenly the dinner happens. The joke is that Susan's excuse was Larry himself, not the dinner. The structural elegance of the callback earns the rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Laura and I are having dinner after the show with her mom. Oh, Diane. Yeah, that's right, Susan. That's right. But listen, that's no reason why the two of you can't go to dinner with each other.
jokes.setup: Goldblum enthusiastically organizes the four-way dinner; Larry has just agreed; Susan is apparently willing now
jokes.punchline: Goldblum immediately reveals the dinner was with Laura and her mom (Diane Ladd) — he won't be there. He's sending Larry and Susan to dinner alone, which is what Larry originally asked for, now facilitated by Goldblum who didn't realize it was needed
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural joke. Goldblum — the guest Larry spent the episode trying to book through proxies — inadvertently becomes the proxy who books Larry's dinner date with Susan. The irony is precise: Larry couldn't ask Susan directly, but Goldblum did it accidentally while not even being available to attend. The show's theme of proxy-mediated social anxiety resolves through a meta-proxy.

jokes.text: And why not? Yes. There we go. Like 2 lovebirds in a cherry tree.
jokes.setup: Goldblum is cheerfully pushing Larry and Susan together
jokes.punchline: 'Like 2 lovebirds in a cherry tree' — a slightly off, overly folksy expression that captures Goldblum's enthusiastic but slightly alien social energy; the phrase is almost right but somehow eccentric
jokes.explanation: A small piece of Goldblum character comedy — the 'cherry tree' is a mild absurdism that works because it's delivered with complete sincerity. The phrase is off in a very specifically Goldblum way.

jokes.text: Next time he's having a fucking nervous breakdown, maybe book David Viscott. Viscott! 2 t's.
jokes.setup: The Goldblum segment in the green room has ended successfully; Artie offers his post-mortem
jokes.punchline: Artie suggests that next time Larry is in an emotional crisis, they should book David Viscott (a pop psychology TV therapist) rather than a movie star — and then pedantically corrects the spelling. The pedantry ('2 t's') is the joke within the joke.
jokes.explanation: A strong Artie line — the suggestion itself is funny (treating Larry's emotional crisis as a booking problem solvable by a TV therapist), and 'Viscott! 2 t's' as an immediate follow-up pedantry is Artie's character in miniature: he's a professional who notices details others miss, including the correct spelling of people he wants to mock-book.

jokes.text: We're lucky to have you here tonight, and I want to thank you for taking time out of your busy schedule to delight us with your... thank you. With my... with what you have.
jokes.setup: Hank is doing an on-air interview with Randy Quaid and attempts a compliment that he can't finish
jokes.punchline: 'With what you have' — Hank loses the thread of his sentence entirely and recovers with the vaguest possible compliment ('with what you have'), which Randy cheerfully completes as if it were perfectly coherent
jokes.explanation: A perfect Hank Kingsley cringe moment. His complete inability to complete a sentence of flattery ends in 'with what you have' — which says nothing while sounding almost like something. Deeply character-specific: Hank is all surface and no substance, and here the surface collapses. Quaid's cooperative 'thank you' makes it worse.

jokes.text: Well, don't mind me. I'm just in the middle of a divorce.
jokes.setup: Hank has stumbled through his intro of Randy Quaid on-air
jokes.punchline: Rather than covering his on-air fumble professionally, Hank announces his divorce to the studio audience mid-interview as an explanation — a completely inappropriate personal overshare dressed as a casual aside
jokes.explanation: A great character comedy moment. The absurdity of announcing your divorce to a studio audience as a mid-interview aside ('Don't mind me') is perfectly Hank — his professional/personal boundaries don't exist. The delivery as a small, offhand, slightly apologetic comment makes it funnier than a big breakdown would. Highly character-specific and quotable.

jokes.text: I'm giving her the Lookaround Cafe. Well, there is a lucky lady. That's wonderful. That's gonna be very successful. Your ex-wife is gonna do very well.
jokes.setup: Hank continues sharing his divorce details on-air; he mentions giving his wife the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Randy Quaid, seemingly sincerely, says the ex-wife is lucky and the restaurant will be very successful — which Hank then undercuts entirely
jokes.explanation: The setup for the bigger crime-restaurant joke. Randy's genuine supportiveness makes the reveal funnier. Functional setup beat.

jokes.text: Well, you should know there was a shooting and a beating and a killing and a stabbing there. Well, they have a competitive side as well.
jokes.setup: Randy Quaid has just said the Lookaround Cafe will be very successful; Hank is taking the 'high road'
jokes.punchline: Hank casually reveals the restaurant has been the site of multiple violent crimes (shooting, beating, killing, stabbing — a deliberate list escalation) and Randy's recovery — 'they have a competitive side as well' — treats violence as a business strategy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The list structure ('a shooting and a beating and a killing and a stabbing') is perfectly escalated — four crimes in ascending severity delivered as a business disclosure. But the real joke is Randy Quaid's comeback: 'they have a competitive side as well' reframes multiple murders as aggressive marketing. The two-person collaborative construction elevates this above a solo bit. Strong dark comedy with excellent character integration (Hank bragging while taking the 'high road') and Randy's game deadpan.

jokes.text: Hey, why don't you come back tomorrow night, and we'll watch the show again. Uh, Larry, I think that maybe... we should keep this relationship just on a professional level, don't you? Oh, yeah. Yes, absolutely. I... that... I'm very comfortable with that.
jokes.setup: Larry and Susan are apparently at/after the dinner that Goldblum inadvertently arranged; it has somehow happened
jokes.punchline: Larry's invitation for Susan to come back 'tomorrow and watch the show again' is another date attempt; Susan's careful 'we should keep this on a professional level' is a clear second rejection; Larry's over-enthusiastic 'Yes, absolutely. I'm very comfortable with that' is the opposite of comfortable
jokes.explanation: A strong character cringe beat. Larry's 'I'm very comfortable with that' when he is visibly not is a quintessential Larry move — performing acceptance of rejection while clearly devastated. The second rejection in the episode reinforces his inability to read signals (or accept them). 'Watch the show again' as a date proposal is also a nicely specific tell about Larry's ego.

jokes.text: Larry, I think that maybe we should keep this relationship just on a professional level, don't you? Oh, yeah. Yes, absolutely. L... that... I'm very comfortable with that.
jokes.setup: Larry has just invited Susan back to watch the show as a romantic gesture
jokes.punchline: Susan promptly suggests keeping it professional; Larry's immediate, over-enthusiastic agreement — 'Oh yeah. Yes, absolutely. I'm very comfortable with that' — reveals how uncomfortable he actually is
jokes.explanation: Larry's aggressively quick agreement that they should stay professional is the classic sitcom overcorrection. The comedy is in the gap between 'very comfortable with that' and the obvious devastation. Good Larry character work but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Christ. I'm sorry that your date didn't work out, but let's just put this all behind us, 'cause we've got a show to do. Don't want to.
jokes.setup: The episode ends with Artie trying to move Larry past the failed date and back to work
jokes.punchline: 'Don't want to' — the final repetition of Larry's petulant refrain, now deployed as the episode's closing beat, landing harder because we know exactly what it means and have seen its arc from sulk to resignation
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and its most structurally satisfying moment. 'Don't want to' has been used twice before; its third appearance as the final line of the episode transforms a running character beat into a thesis statement. Larry is a man who runs a show he doesn't want to do, pursues relationships he can't maintain, and refuses to grow — and 'don't want to' encapsulates all of this in three words. The running gag payoff earns the high structure and character integration scores. This is the kind of closing beat that defines a show's identity.

tmdb_overview: Paula has trouble booking guests for sweeps week, so she leans on Larry to ask his friend Jeff Goldblum, who in turn offers to help Larry get a date with a network publicist.
